_about.what: The divisions inside a corps, as both interfaces show them: what each kind is called, the numbers they carry, and how a corps' strength and experience are shared out among its divisions.
_about.rule: A corps fights as one body: its strength and its experience are the corps' own, and the divisions shown inside it always add up to exactly those. Each division keeps its own character through the war, so the same one is always the most worn or the most seasoned of its corps. Nothing here changes a battle.
_about.kinds: For each kind of corps: 'word' as it reads in a count ('5 infantry divisions'), 'name' for one division ('7th Infantry Division') and 'short' for a card.
_about.names: What a nation calls its own divisions of a kind, where it differs: [name, short].
_about.historic: The divisions a corps of the 1939 order of battle (setup-1939.json) actually had, by nation and corps name, in its own order: [name, short]. A division past the end of a list, or of a corps not listed, takes its nation's number for its kind. From the historian, for the field battles (the design director, b358). A division whose kind the corps does not hold is left to its number (b371: I Corps' third, Panzer Division Kempf, waits until the corps holds armour).
_about.reads: The divisions a formation's own name gives, by nation and formation name, where the name alone does not read as its record does (the design director, 13:48Z, 13:50Z and 14:28Z of 25 November 2026, on the historian's named-twice-reads-1125.md; no row is renamed, since a row's name is its key). One division, one name for life: New Zealand's is the 'New Zealand Division' in every row, the name its first row gives. An American division carries its arm (the '5th Infantry Division'; a bare '5th' in a list of British divisions is the British 5th). A different army's unit carries that army's name (the Chinese 50th is not Britain's 50th). A part is not a division: a brigade, a regiment or a detachment laid as a row of its own reads as itself, never as the whole division it belongs to. Nor is a row of one division that stands for several of another army's a list of them: it reads as one, under its own name (a Chinese army of three small divisions, laid as one). Read after 'historic', before the name itself.
_about.order: The order the kinds are listed in when an army is summed up.
_about.spread: How far apart the divisions of a corps stand: the share of the room the corps' own strength (or experience) leaves either side of it.
_about.hardened: The experience (0 to 1) at which a division counts as battle-hardened.
_about.record: Real division numbers of 1939 that no first-day corps carries (setup-1939.json's 'nos' holds those that do), by nation and arm, from the historian's divisions-1939-ger.md (18 November 2026): divisions in no corps that day, and those of another arm than the game's corps. A stand-in division is numbered from above the highest real number of its nation's arm, so that no stand-in ever takes a real number and no name is carried twice (the design director, 18 November).
